analysis.one_liner: Lets states create their own universal health care systems using existing federal health funding.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Senator Markey with three Democratic cosponsors, has had no committee action since it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in July 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Affordable Care Act to let any state apply for a waiver to set up its own universal, publicly administered health care system. The state would fold together federal money it currently receives through Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, the ACA marketplaces, premium tax credits, federal employee coverage, and TRICARE, and use it to run a single state plan covering all residents. States would have to reach at least 95 percent coverage within five years, keep benefits and cost protections at least as good as the federal programs they replace, and make the plan budget-neutral for the federal government.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of any state that chooses to adopt a plan: the uninsured, people on Medicaid or marketplace plans facing high deductibles, and people priced out of private coverage. The bill requires coverage of reproductive health care including abortion, contraception, and gender-affirming care, and requires the state plan to be publicly administered rather than run by private insurers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents of states that opt in

how_it_helps.text: A state plan must cover all residents and be at least as comprehensive and affordable as the federal programs it replaces, including Medicaid's mandatory benefits.

The state receives the full amount of federal health dollars that would otherwise be spent on its residents, including premium tax credits and administrative funds, adjusted for caseload growth and medical inflation, and keeps any savings for reinvestment in health care.
The plan must be publicly administered by a state agency or independent public entity, and the state must restrict the sale of duplicative or supplemental private insurance.

Waiver applications face public notice and comment, an independent review panel that includes patient advocates, nurses, and rural and primary care providers, and five-year reviews with public hearings on coverage, affordability, and quality.
States can team up regionally on a single application, and tribal consultation rules protect American Indian and Alaska Native health programs.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government pays out the same aggregate amount it spends today, by design. The gap between that funding and the full cost of universal coverage falls on the state, which must find its own revenue, likely through new taxes. Private insurers lose premium revenue and employers would no longer need to sponsor coverage in participating states, shifting their role to the state plan.
analysis.who_pays_short: Participating states' taxpayers and private insurers

drawbacks.text: The waiver must be budget-neutral for the federal government, so a state has to finance whatever the passthrough does not cover, meaning significant new state revenue, likely taxes, to reach universal coverage.
A state must reach at least 95 percent coverage within five years, with a 12-month grace period; a state that still falls short can have its waiver terminated by the Secretary.
Residents would lose the specific coverage they have today, including employer plans and private marketplace plans, in exchange for the state plan, which some would prefer to keep.
The bill only matters if a state actually enacts such a plan; no state currently has a universal publicly administered system in effect, so the federal waiver alone changes nothing on its own.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For uninsured and underinsured residents of a participating state, the potential gain is large: guaranteed comprehensive coverage with cost protections. The cost is real but borne unevenly: state taxpayers would fund the difference between federal passthrough dollars and actual program cost, and the plan's fate depends entirely on a state legislature choosing to act. The design includes genuine guardrails, five-year reviews, public comment, and waiver termination for failure, but it also gives the federal Secretary wide discretion to set and revoke terms.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2025, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Senator Markey introduced the bill on July 15, 2025, with Senators Warren, Merkley, and Padilla as cosponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that is the last action on record.

The bill would create a new ACA section 1335 waiver letting states pool funding from Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, ACA subsidies, federal employee and military health coverage, and ERISA into one publicly administered universal state plan.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nothing has changed: private insurers, employers, and the existing patchwork of federal and private coverage continue as they are.

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the State-Based Universal Health Care Act of 2025 and referred it to Senate Finance.

for.name: Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Ron Wyden ally Ron Merkley, and Alex Padilla
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's three cosponsors; none is on the Finance Committee route to advance it alone.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee of referral
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled any hearing or markup on the bill since its referral in July 2025, leaving it without a path to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors are Democrats and the bill has no Republican cosponsors; with Republicans chairing Senate Finance and holding the majority, the committee has taken no action.

industries.note: A state plan must be publicly administered and the state must restrict the sale of duplicative or supplemental private coverage, so insurers in an opting-in state would lose the individual, marketplace, Medicaid managed care, and employer premium business that the state plan replaces.

Employers in a participating state could stop offering coverage and let the state plan take over, saving them premium costs, but their employees would trade familiar private plans for the state system.
A universal state plan would guarantee providers a patient base and cut uncompensated care, but state plans typically pay lower rates than private insurance, so revenue per patient could fall.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans controlling the Senate and chairing the Finance Committee, and no Republican cosponsors, the bill is very unlikely to get a hearing, markup, or floor vote this Congress; the realistic path is that it sits in committee until the session ends, as similar state-single-payer waiver bills have in prior years.
